inclusion_rule: Studies that recognize phones, words or sentences as text from non-acoustic speech-production signals measured on the speaker (ultrasound, surface or intramuscular EMG, EMA/PMA or magnetic sensing, EPG, radar, ECoG, intracortical, EEG/MEG), classified by full-text pattern (reference list removed) by recognizer family: HMM (with GMM or other emission models), neural network, SVM, DTW. Boundary: exclude studies whose recognizer takes acoustic input at test (AVSR with audio, NAM or whisper microphones, acoustic-to-articulatory inversion), lip-video-only lipreading, perception or neuroscience studies without a recognizer, and reviews; versions of one study count once; earlier versions of the target system are merged with the target.

usual_approach.design: HMM recognizer (GMM emissions) on frame features, at the target time (2009-11)
usual_approach.note: dated: 10 of 12 prior unique studies use an HMM recognizer (8 EMG, 2 EMA/EPG); an EEG word classifier and an EMG neural-network vowel recognizer (Manabe 2003) do not; all-years population of 118 unique studies (pattern match): neural network 81, HMM 60, SVM 36, DTW 15

read_fulltext.quote: Rate of 6.17% is obtained with DCAE, compared to the

The trained acoustic model was used together with a trigram BN
language model for decoding.

Each phoneme is modeled using a 3-state left-to-right Hidden Markov Model (beginning, middle, and end
of the phoneme), silence is modeled by a single state.
Since the training set is very small, we only trained context-independent acoustic models.
the system is able to correctly identify 65,6% of the phones from visual information only
We followed the same setting for the whole recognition system as in [1], except with different feature extraction methods.
We used a three-layer neural network with 3 input layer nodes, 6 hidden layer nodes, and 5 output layer nodes, each of which corresponds to one of the 5 Japanese vowels.
